newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl under pressure as debate over euro rages.
newsitem.headline: Kohl under pressure as debate over euro rages.

text.p: As Germany continued splitting hairs on Sunday over the membership criteria for Europe's planned single currency, cracks in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat party appeared to widen.

Kohl is under pressure to counter a vocal campaign by Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber who is calling for a delay to monetary union if the entry criteria are weakened, and he must restore coalition unity to get budget reforms back on track.

Edmund Stoiber, an influential member of the conservative Christial Social Union (CSU), ran from one interview to the next, threatening to block German membership of monetary union in the upper house unless the criteria are strictly met.
"If the requirements are not fulfilled then, of course, we will have to agree on a thorough, controlled postponement," Stoiber told the weekly Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
In an interview with German Radio, he said: "The criteria determine the timetable and not the other way around."

"If you say the euro must come on January 1, 1999 as agreed and basically no longer say the criteria determine the timetable, then of course you create the impression that the criteria are considered less important than the timetable."

The CSU is sister party to Kohl's larger Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Together they form the ruling coaltion with the liberal Free Democrats (FDP). One senior CSU official threatened to end the alliance with Kohl's CDU over the euro.
Prospective members of economic and monetary union (EMU) must limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 to qualify for the single currency in 1999.

With European Union members Germany and France in danger of missing the deficit target, discussion is raging over how to interpret the three percent limit and whether postponing EMU might do more damage than allowing slightly higher deficits.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, urging the government to complete its comprehensive tax reform plan, in an interview with Hesse Radio said a commitment to lasting stability was more important for EMU than meeting the deficit target.
"The three percent is an important reference number -- there is no doubt of that," he said.

"But more important than the one-off fulfilment, or bare undershooting or overshooting of this number, is the question as to whether countries' public finances are in a condition that can be viewed as sustainable, and lastingly sustainable."

The subtle difference is one of the hottest debates going in the run-up to monetary union. Should a country like Germany, which has a long track record of fiscal discipline, be kept out of EMU because its budget deficit slightly exceeds the target?
Jean-Claude Juncker, the Luxembourg prime minister who takes over the European Union presidency this week, said he expected Germany to join EMU even if its deficit was too high.

"If a member temporarily veers from this reference value but then clearly moves in the direction of the value again and it has committed itself lastingly to stability, then even 3.2 percent conforms to the treaty," he said.

The other side of the question is whether a country such as Italy, which does not have a long record of fiscal prudence, should be allowed into the EMU club if it is able to squeeze into the Maastricht corset this year.
Many conservatives like Stoiber fear that if an exception is made for Germany or France, then exceptions will have to be made for other countries as well.

"If we begin with 3.2, then come the next ones with 3.6 and the next country with 3.8 or 3.9. That says everything. If we begin to waver then we should know that three percent meanwhile has become synonomous with monetary stability," said Stoiber.
But the Bavarian premier, a rival of CSU chief Theo Waigel, Kohl's finance minister in Bonn, has been accused of launching an anti-euro campaign to improve his political profile.

Otto Lambsdorff, a senior FDP economics expert, told Welt am Sonntag that for Stoiber "other considerations" played a significant role in his euro comments -- "Party and electoral considerations, differences between the CDU and CSU as well as the unmistakable conflict between Stoiber and Waigel."
A poll in this week's Der Spiegel news magazine showed that sixty percent of Germans polled do not believe that monetary union will start on time, while 39 percent believed it would.
